claim: Acute lymphoblastic and myeloblastic leukemias (ALL and AML) modify the bone marrow microenvironment and disrupt non-malignant hematopoiesis.
source: Acute lymphoblastic and myeloblastic leukemias (ALL and AML) have been known to modify the bone marrow microenvironment and disrupt non-malignant hematopoiesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract introduction.

claim: The molecular mechanisms driving leukemia-induced alterations in the bone marrow microenvironment remain poorly defined.
source: However, the molecular mechanisms driving these alterations remain poorly defined.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: Leukemic cells turn off lymphopoiesis and erythropoiesis shortly after colonizing the bone marrow.
source: Using mouse models of ALL and AML, here we show that leukemic cells turn off lymphopoiesis and erythropoiesis shortly after colonizing the bone marrow.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: ALL and AML cells express lymphotoxin α1β2.
source: ALL and AML cells express lymphotoxin α1β2 and activate lymphotoxin beta receptor (LTβR) signaling in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), which turns off IL7 production and prevents non-malignant lymphopoiesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by flow cytometry data in Figures 2A-B and 6A.

claim: ALL and AML cells activate lymphotoxin beta receptor (LTβR) signaling in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs).
source: ALL and AML cells express lymphotoxin α1β2 and activate lymphotoxin beta receptor (LTβR) signaling in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), which turns off IL7 production and prevents non-malignant lymphopoiesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing IL7 downregulation that is LTβR-dependent.

claim: LTβR signaling in MSCs turns off IL7 production.
source: ALL and AML cells express lymphotoxin α1β2 and activate lymphotoxin beta receptor (LTβR) signaling in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), which turns off IL7 production and prevents non-malignant lymphopoiesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2D, 3D, 4B, and 6B showing IL7 downregulation that is reversed by LTβR blocking.

claim: LTβR signaling prevents non-malignant lymphopoiesis.
source: ALL and AML cells express lymphotoxin α1β2 and activate lymphotoxin beta receptor (LTβR) signaling in mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs), which turns off IL7 production and prevents non-malignant lymphopoiesis.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2D, 4C-E showing restoration of lymphopoiesis when LTβR signaling is blocked.

claim: The DNA damage response pathway promotes lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in leukemic cells.
source: We show that the DNA damage response pathway and CXCR4 signaling promote lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in leukemic cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-H showing Etoposide-induced LTα upregulation.

claim: CXCR4 signaling promotes lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in leukemic cells.
source: We show that the DNA damage response pathway and CXCR4 signaling promote lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in leukemic cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 5A-D showing CXCL12-induced LTα upregulation.

claim: Genetic disruption of LTβR signaling in MSCs restores lymphopoiesis but not erythropoiesis.
source: Genetic or pharmacological disruption of LTβR signaling in MSCs restores lymphopoiesis but not erythropoiesis, reduces leukemic cell growth, and significantly extends the survival of transplant recipients.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2D-E, 4C-J showing selective restoration of lymphopoiesis.

claim: Pharmacological disruption of LTβR signaling in MSCs restores lymphopoiesis but not erythropoiesis.
source: Genetic or pharmacological disruption of LTβR signaling in MSCs restores lymphopoiesis but not erythropoiesis, reduces leukemic cell growth, and significantly extends the survival of transplant recipients.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2D-E showing selective restoration of lymphopoiesis with LTβR-Ig treatment.

claim: Disruption of LTβR signaling in MSCs reduces leukemic cell growth.
source: Genetic or pharmacological disruption of LTβR signaling in MSCs restores lymphopoiesis but not erythropoiesis, reduces leukemic cell growth, and significantly extends the survival of transplant recipients.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 2H, 4F, 4K, 4P, 6E showing reduced ALL/AML numbers.

claim: Disruption of LTβR signaling in MSCs significantly extends the survival of transplant recipients.
source: Genetic or pharmacological disruption of LTβR signaling in MSCs restores lymphopoiesis but not erythropoiesis, reduces leukemic cell growth, and significantly extends the survival of transplant recipients.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by survival data in Figures 2I, 4L, 4Q, 6F, 6G.

claim: CXCR4 blocking prevents leukemia-induced IL7 downregulation.
source: Similarly, CXCR4 blocking also prevents leukemia-induced IL7 downregulation and inhibits leukemia growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 5F showing maintained IL7 expression with CXCR4 antagonist treatment.

claim: CXCR4 blocking inhibits leukemia growth.
source: Similarly, CXCR4 blocking also prevents leukemia-induced IL7 downregulation and inhibits leukemia growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 5H-I showing reduced ALL numbers and extended survival.

claim: Acute leukemias exploit physiological mechanisms governing hematopoietic output as a strategy for gaining competitive advantage.
source: These studies demonstrate that acute leukemias exploit physiological mechanisms governing hematopoietic output as a strategy for gaining competitive advantage.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, inferred from the collective experimental findings.

claim: All blood cells develop from a dedicated hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) that colonizes specialized niches in the bone marrow formed predominantly by mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and endothelial cells (ECs).
source: All blood cells develop from a dedicated hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) that colonizes specialized niches in the bone marrow (BM) formed predominantly by mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and endothelial cells (ECs) (Morrison and Scadden, 2014; Pinho and Frenette, 2019; Sugiyama et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HSCs and hematopoietic progenitors receive critical signals for long-term HSC maintenance and for differentiation into lymphoid, myeloid, and erythroid lineages within bone marrow niches.
source: Within these niches, HSCs and hematopoietic progenitors receive critical signals for long-term HSC maintenance and for differentiation into lymphoid, myeloid, and erythroid lineages (Sugiyama et al., 2019; Miao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most hematopoietic cytokines act in a short-range manner.
source: However, most hematopoietic cytokines act in a short-range manner, and thus hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells rely on localization cues such as CXCL12 for accessing growth factors produced by MSCs and ECs (Noda et al., 2011; Tzeng et al., 2011; Ding and Morrison, 2013; Greenbaum et al., 2013; Cordeiro Gomes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells rely on localization cues such as CXCL12 for accessing growth factors produced by MSCs and ECs.
source: However, most hematopoietic cytokines act in a short-range manner, and thus hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells rely on localization cues such as CXCL12 for accessing growth factors produced by MSCs and ECs (Noda et al., 2011; Tzeng et al., 2011; Ding and Morrison, 2013; Greenbaum et al., 2013; Cordeiro Gomes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: HSCs and uncommitted hematopoietic progenitors are critically dependent on stem cell factor (SCF, encoded by Kitl).
source: While HSCs and uncommitted hematopoietic progenitors are critically dependent on stem cell factor (SCF, encoded by Kitl), committed progenitors require lineage-specific signals, such as IL7 for lymphocytes, IL15 for NK cells, or M-CSF for monocytes and macrophages.
evidence: This is established knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: Committed progenitors require lineage-specific signals, such as IL7 for lymphocytes, IL15 for NK cells, or M-CSF for monocytes and macrophages.
source: While HSCs and uncommitted hematopoietic progenitors are critically dependent on stem cell factor (SCF, encoded by Kitl), committed progenitors require lineage-specific signals, such as IL7 for lymphocytes, IL15 for NK cells, or M-CSF for monocytes and macrophages.
evidence: This is established knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: Most hematopoietic cytokines are produced by MSCs and by a subset of ECs in the BM.
source: Importantly, most hematopoietic cytokines are produced by MSCs and by a subset of ECs in the BM (Miao et al., 2020; Noda et al., 2011; Cordeiro Gomes et al., 2016; Ding et al., 2012; Baryawno et al., 2019; Comazzetto et al., 2019; Tikhonova et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The production of hematopoietic cytokines and chemokines by MSCs and ECs is relatively stable during homeostasis but can change significantly under certain perturbations.
source: The production of hematopoietic cytokines and chemokines by MSCs and ECs is relatively stable during homeostasis but can change significantly under certain perturbations.
evidence: This is established knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: Systemic inflammation caused by infections enforces the downregulation of multiple hematopoietic cytokines and CXCL12 in the BM.
source: For example, systemic inflammation caused by infections enforces the downregulation of multiple hematopoietic cytokines and CXCL12 in the BM (Ueda et al., 2004; Ueda et al., 2005; Manz and Boettcher, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Acute lymphoblastic and myeloblastic leukemias (ALL and AML) promote the downregulation of multiple cytokines and CXCL12 produced by MSCs and ECs.
source: Likewise, acute lymphoblastic and myeloblastic leukemias (ALL and AML) also promote the downregulation of multiple cytokines and CXCL12 produced by MSCs and ECs (Baryawno et al., 2019; Hanoun et al., 2014; Fistonich et al., 2018; Zehentmeier and Pereira, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: During systemic infection, the coordinated downregulation of certain cytokines (e.g. IL7) and CXCL12 causes a temporary pause in lymphopoiesis that is necessary for an emergent production of short-lived neutrophils and monocytes.
source: During systemic infection, the coordinated downregulation of certain cytokines (e.g. IL7) and CXCL12 causes a temporary pause in lymphopoiesis that is necessary for an emergent production of short-lived neutrophils and monocytes (Manz and Boettcher, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In leukemic states, the mechanism(s) promoting cytokine and chemokine downregulation are not well defined.
source: In leukemic states, however, the mechanism(s) promoting cytokine and chemokine downregulation are not well defined, and neither is known if these changes are protective or harmful for the host.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: It is not known if leukemia-induced changes in cytokine and chemokine expression are protective or harmful for the host.
source: In leukemic states, however, the mechanism(s) promoting cytokine and chemokine downregulation are not well defined, and neither is known if these changes are protective or harmful for the host.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: In humans and in mouse models of B-ALL, leukemic cells use CXCR4 to home to the BM.
source: In humans and in mouse models of B-ALL, leukemic cells use CXCR4 to home to the BM (Juarez et al., 2007; Colmone et al., 2008; van den Berk et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: B-ALL cells do not distribute randomly and seem to reside and proliferate in certain perivascular niches.
source: However, B-ALL cells do not distribute randomly and seem to reside and proliferate in certain perivascular niches (Colmone et al., 2008; Sipkins et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CXCL12 production is measurably reduced exclusively in BM niches colonized by B-ALL cells.
source: Importantly, CXCL12 production is measurably reduced exclusively in BM niches colonized by B-ALL cells (Colmone et al., 2008; van den Berk et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Intact CXCR4 signaling presumably in B-ALL cells is required for downregulation of CXCL12 expression in BM niche cells.
source: Furthermore, intact CXCR4 signaling presumably in B-ALL cells is required for downregulation of CXCL12 expression in BM niche cells (van den Berk et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: CXCR4 expression levels in B-ALL cells inversely correlate with patient outcome.
source: The fact that CXCR4 expression levels in B-ALL cells inversely correlate with patient outcome suggests that B-ALL-induced changes in the BM microenvironment may favor leukemia progression (van den Berk et al., 2014; Cancilla et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: B-ALL-induced changes in the BM microenvironment may favor leukemia progression.
source: The fact that CXCR4 expression levels in B-ALL cells inversely correlate with patient outcome suggests that B-ALL-induced changes in the BM microenvironment may favor leukemia progression (van den Berk et al., 2014; Cancilla et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on cited literature.

claim: The BM microenvironment is severely affected in AML patients and in mouse models of AML.
source: The BM microenvironment has also been reported to be severely affected in AML patients and in mouse models of AML.
evidence: This is established knowledge stated in the introduction.

claim: Hematopoietic cytokines and chemokines are significantly downregulated along with the re-programing of MSC and EC transcriptomes in AML.
source: Of note, hematopoietic cytokines and chemokines are significantly downregulated along with the re-programing of MSC and EC transcriptomes (Baryawno et al., 2019; Hanoun et al., 2014; Chandran et al., 2015; Geyh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: No specific mechanisms have been identified for explaining how AML cells dysregulate MSCs and ECs.
source: Although no specific mechanisms have been identified for explaining how AML cells dysregulate MSCs and ECs, some evidence suggests that this may be mediated by direct AML-niche cell interactions (Hérault et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: AML-induced dysregulation of MSCs and ECs may be mediated by direct AML-niche cell interactions.
source: Although no specific mechanisms have been identified for explaining how AML cells dysregulate MSCs and ECs, some evidence suggests that this may be mediated by direct AML-niche cell interactions (Hérault et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Leukemia cells attracted to CXCL12-producing BM niches physically interact and re-program MSCs and ECs to reduce CXCL12 levels, possibly reduce hematopoietic output, and in this way favor leukemic cell expansion.
source: Thus, a model emerges where leukemia cells attracted to CXCL12-producing BM niches physically interact and re-program MSCs and ECs to reduce CXCL12 levels, possibly reduce hematopoietic output, and in this way favor leukemic cell expansion.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed based on prior observations.

claim: The molecular mechanisms utilized by leukemia for MSC and EC re-programing and for reducing non-malignant hematopoiesis remain poorly defined.
source: However, the molecular mechanisms utilized by leukemia for MSC and EC re-programing and for reducing non-malignant hematopoiesis remain poorly defined.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: ALL cells expanded rapidly in BM after transplantation into non-irradiated C57Bl6/J mice.
source: As expected, ALL cells expanded rapidly in BM (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Non-leukemic developing B cells and mature recirculating B cells declined sharply 2 weeks after ALL transplantation.
source: Conversely, non-leukemic developing B cells and mature recirculating B cells declined sharply 2 weeks after ALL transplantation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Monocyte numbers reduced between the first and second weeks by four- to fivefold, but cell numbers recovered to normal levels at 3 weeks after ALL transplantation.
source: Monocyte numbers reduced between the first and second weeks by four- to fivefold, but cell numbers recovered to normal levels at 3 weeks (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Neutrophil numbers showed a moderate twofold decline at 2 weeks that remained stable until 3 weeks after ALL transplantation.
source: This contrasted with a moderate twofold decline in neutrophil numbers at 2 weeks that remained stable until 3 weeks (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Immature erythrocytes (Ter119+CD71+ cells) progressively reduced at 6, 14, and 21 days after ALL transplantation, reaching >10-fold reductions at 3 weeks.
source: Changes in immature erythrocytes (Ter119+CD71+ cells) were similar to the reductions seen in B cell progenitors: erythroid cells progressively reduced at 6, 14, and 21 days after ALL transplantation, reaching >10-fold reductions at 3 weeks (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: ALL expansion induces a strong decline in lymphopoiesis and erythropoiesis while their impact on myeloid cell production is modest.
source: In summary, ALL expansion induces a strong decline in lymphopoiesis and erythropoiesis while their impact on myeloid cell production is modest.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data from Figure 1.

claim: Transplanted ALL cells and Artemis-deficient (pre-leukemic) pre-B cells led to IL7 and CXCL12 downregulation in MSCs.
source: In previous studies we noted that transplanted ALL cells and Artemis-deficient (pre-leukemic) pre-B cells led to IL7 and CXCL12 downregulation in MSCs (Fistonich et al., 2018), which could explain the negative impact of ALL in non-malignant lymphopoiesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: LTβR signaling in BM stromal cells plays a role in development of some lymphoid lineages.
source: While the mechanism(s) responsible for IL7 and CXCL12 downregulation remained undefined, earlier studies suggested a role for LTβR signaling in BM stromal cells in development of some lymphoid lineages (Wu et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MSCs express LTβR.
source: In recent studies, we found that MSCs express LTβR and that LTβR signaling controls IL7 expression in vivo (Zehentmeier et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: LTβR signaling controls IL7 expression in vivo.
source: In recent studies, we found that MSCs express LTβR and that LTβR signaling controls IL7 expression in vivo (Zehentmeier et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: LTB transcript abundance inversely correlates with relapse-free survival in pediatric B-ALL patients at the time of diagnosis.
source: Furthermore, when mRNA levels of LTB were analyzed in pediatric samples of B-ALL (Children's Oncology Group Study 9906 for High-Risk Pediatric ALL) and associated with clinical outcome at the time of diagnosis, we noted an inverse correlation between LTB transcript abundance and relapse-free survival that reached statistical significance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A analyzing patient samples.

claim: BCR-ABL1 expressing pre-B ALL cells express higher LTα/LTβ amounts than non-leukemic pre-B, immature, and mature B cells.
source: In mice, BCR-ABL1 expressing pre-B ALL cells also express higher LTα/LTβ amounts than non-leukemic pre-B, immature, and mature B cells (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: The presence of ALL cells in the BM environment did not change LTα and LTβ expression on non-leukemic host pre-B cells.
source: The presence of ALL cells in the BM environment did not change LTα and LTβ expression on non-leukemic host pre-B cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mouse ALL cells engineered to over-express LTα/LTβ induced stronger IL7 downregulation in BM MSCs than empty vector transduced ALL cells.
source: Importantly, when mouse ALL cells were engineered to over-express LTα/LTβ, these ALLs induced stronger IL7 downregulation in BM MSCs and were lethal more quickly than empty vector transduced ALL cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: Mouse ALL cells engineered to over-express LTα/LTβ were lethal more quickly than empty vector transduced ALL cells.
source: Importantly, when mouse ALL cells were engineered to over-express LTα/LTβ, these ALLs induced stronger IL7 downregulation in BM MSCs and were lethal more quickly than empty vector transduced ALL cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–E).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: LTβR-Ig treatment reverted ALL-induced reduction in lymphopoiesis.
source: Transplanted ALL cells reduced lymphopoiesis significantly, which was reverted with LTβR-Ig treatment (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: LTβR signaling blockade did not restore erythropoiesis or myelopoiesis in ALL-transplanted mice.
source: In contrast, LTβR signaling blockade did not restore erythropoiesis or myelopoiesis (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 2E-G.

claim: ALL growth was significantly reduced at 2 weeks with LTβR-Ig treatment.
source: Importantly, ALL growth was significantly reduced at 2 weeks (Figure 2H), which reflected in a small but significant extension of mouse survival (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: LTβR-Ig treatment resulted in a small but significant extension of mouse survival after ALL transplantation.
source: Importantly, ALL growth was significantly reduced at 2 weeks (Figure 2H), which reflected in a small but significant extension of mouse survival (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: ALL growth in vivo induced major transcriptional changes in MSCs.
source: Samples from control and ALL groups separated by PC1, and within ALL cohorts, samples from LTβR-Ig versus Hel-Ig treated ALL also segregated from each other, thus indicating major transcriptional changes induced by ALL growth in vivo, of which a significant fraction was sensitive to LTβR blocking (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A significant fraction of ALL-induced transcriptional changes in MSCs was sensitive to LTβR blocking.
source: Samples from control and ALL groups separated by PC1, and within ALL cohorts, samples from LTβR-Ig versus Hel-Ig treated ALL also segregated from each other, thus indicating major transcriptional changes induced by ALL growth in vivo, of which a significant fraction was sensitive to LTβR blocking (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by PCA data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Comparisons between control and ALL treated with Hel-Ig samples revealed 322 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; Padj <0.05, |log2FC|>1), of which 74 were downregulated and 248 were upregulated in MSCs of control mice.
source: Comparisons between control and ALL treated with Hel-Ig samples revealed 322 differentially expressed genes (DEGs; Padj <0.05, |log2FC|>1), of which 74 were downregulated and 248 were upregulated in MSCs of control mice (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: Comparisons between the ALL groups (Hel-Ig versus LTβR-Ig) revealed 226 DEGs of which 149 were upregulated and 77 were downregulated in MSCs of mice with ALL and treated with Hel-Ig.
source: Comparisons between the ALL groups (Hel-Ig versus LTβR-Ig) revealed 226 DEGs of which 149 were upregulated and 77 were downregulated in MSCs of mice with ALL and treated with Hel-Ig (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis results.

claim: ALL induced a strong inflammatory gene signature in MSCs with strong statistical significance in interferon α- and γ-induced genes, complement, and cytokines IL2, IL6, and TNFα signaling.
source: Gene set enrichment analyses revealed a strong inflammatory gene signature induced by ALL with a strong statistical significance in interferon α- and γ-induced genes, complement, and cytokines IL2, IL6, and TNFα signaling (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LTβR blocking further increased the interferon stimulated gene signature in MSCs.
source: Of note, LTβR blocking further increased the interferon stimulated gene signature, while it reduced the expression of genes associated with TNFα signaling (Figure 3C), consistent with the fact that LTβR is a TNF superfamily member that activates canonical and non-canonical nuclear factor kappa-binding transcription factors (NFκB) (Norris and Ware, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: LTβR blocking reduced the expression of genes associated with TNFα signaling in MSCs.
source: Of note, LTβR blocking further increased the interferon stimulated gene signature, while it reduced the expression of genes associated with TNFα signaling (Figure 3C), consistent with the fact that LTβR is a TNF superfamily member that activates canonical and non-canonical nuclear factor kappa-binding transcription factors (NFκB) (Norris and Ware, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 3C and is consistent with known LTβR signaling pathways.

claim: LTβR is a TNF superfamily member that activates canonical and non-canonical nuclear factor kappa-binding transcription factors (NFκB).
source: Of note, LTβR blocking further increased the interferon stimulated gene signature, while it reduced the expression of genes associated with TNFα signaling (Figure 3C), consistent with the fact that LTβR is a TNF superfamily member that activates canonical and non-canonical nuclear factor kappa-binding transcription factors (NFκB) (Norris and Ware, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: KITL, IL7, IGF1, and CSF1 were significantly downregulated by ALL cells in MSCs.
source: Importantly, of the several hematopoietic cytokines expressed by MSCs, KITL, IL7, IGF1, and CSF1 were significantly downregulated by ALL cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: ALL-induced transcriptional changes in MSCs were similar to those described in mice with acute myeloid leukemia.
source: These transcriptional changes in MSCs were similar to those described in mice with acute myeloid leukemia (Baryawno et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature supported by citation.

claim: Of the hematopoietic cytokines downregulated by ALL, only IL7 downregulation was blocked by LTβR-Ig treatment.
source: However, of these hematopoietic cytokines, only IL7 downregulation was blocked by LTβR-Ig treatment (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Blocking TNFα and IL1β did not prevent IL7 downregulation nor did it rescue non-malignant lymphopoiesis or myelopoiesis.
source: Furthermore, blocking other NFκB-inducing cytokines, such as TNFα and IL1β, did not prevent IL7 downregulation nor did it rescue non-malignant lymphopoiesis or myelopoiesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C) and did not impact ALL expansion in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Blocking TNFα and IL1β did not impact ALL expansion in vivo.
source: Furthermore, blocking other NFκB-inducing cytokines, such as TNFα and IL1β, did not prevent IL7 downregulation nor did it rescue non-malignant lymphopoiesis or myelopoiesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C) and did not impact ALL expansion in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Blocking IFNα or IFNγ signaling did not rescue IL7 downregulation and non-malignant hematopoiesis, nor did it reduce ALL growth in vivo.
source: Even though ALL cells promoted an interferon-induced gene expression signature in MSCs (Figure 3C), blocking IFNα or IFNγ signaling did not rescue IL7 downregulation and non-malignant hematopoiesis, nor did it reduce ALL growth in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-I.

claim: LTβR signaling in MSCs does not control CXCL12 expression under homeostatic conditions.
source: We ruled out a role for LTβR signaling in MSCs in promoting ALL homing to the BM by transplanting 3×106 ALL cells into control or LTβR∆ mice (Figure 4A), in agreement with prior studies showing that LTβR signaling in MSCs does not control CXCL12 expression under homeostatic conditions (Zehentmeier et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and by citation to prior work.

claim: Transplanted ALL cells induced IL7 downregulation in control mice but not in LTβR∆ mice.
source: Transplanted ALL cells induced IL7 downregulation in control mice (WT, Lepr+/+; Ltbrfl/fl) but not in LTβR∆ mice (Figure 4B), as expected (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Changes in IL7 production corresponded with reduced lymphopoiesis in WT mice whereas lymphopoiesis was largely unaffected in LTβR∆ mice.
source: These changes in IL7 production corresponded with reduced lymphopoiesis in WT mice whereas lymphopoiesis was largely unaffected in LTβR∆ mice (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4C-E.

claim: ALL-induced reductions in myeloid and erythroid lineages were largely independent of LTβR signaling in MSCs.
source: In contrast, ALL-induced reductions in myeloid and erythroid lineages were largely independent of LTβR signaling in MSCs (Figure 4G–J).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4G-J.

claim: The inability to induce LTβR signaling in MSCs impacted ALL growth in vivo.
source: The inability to induce LTβR signaling in MSCs also impacted ALL growth in vivo (Figure 4F and K) such that it extended mouse survival by approximately 1 week (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4F, 4K, and 4L.

claim: The inability to induce LTβR signaling in MSCs extended mouse survival by approximately 1 week after ALL transplantation.
source: The inability to induce LTβR signaling in MSCs also impacted ALL growth in vivo (Figure 4F and K) such that it extended mouse survival by approximately 1 week (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Ltb-deficient ALL cells were unable to induce IL7 downregulation in MSCs and to block non-malignant lymphopoiesis.
source: Indeed, Ltb-deficient ALL cells were unable to induce IL7 downregulation in MSCs and to block non-malignant lymphopoiesis (Figure 4N and O).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4N and 4O.

claim: Ltb-deficient ALL cells proliferated significantly less than Ltb-sufficient ALL cells.
source: Furthermore, Ltb-deficient ALL cells proliferated significantly less than Ltb-sufficient ALL cells (Figure 4P), which extended mouse survival significantly (Figure 4Q).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4P.

claim: Ltb-deficient ALL cells extended mouse survival significantly compared to Ltb-sufficient ALL cells.
source: Furthermore, Ltb-deficient ALL cells proliferated significantly less than Ltb-sufficient ALL cells (Figure 4P), which extended mouse survival significantly (Figure 4Q).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 4Q.

claim: IL7 expression was unchanged even in mice transplanted with threefold higher number of Ltb-deficient ALLs.
source: Importantly, IL7 expression was unchanged even in mice transplanted with threefold higher number of Ltb-deficient ALLs (Figure 4R and S).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 4R and 4S.

claim: ALL-induced IL7 downregulation is mediated by direct delivery of lymphotoxin ligands to LTβR expressed on BM MSCs.
source: Combined, these studies show that the ALL-induced IL7 downregulation that we reported in previous studies (Fistonich et al., 2018; Zehentmeier and Pereira, 2019) is mediated by direct delivery of lymphotoxin ligands to LTβR expressed on BM MSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the collective experimental data in Figures 2-4.

claim: Mice treated with IL7/aIL7 had significantly higher numbers of developing B cell subsets in the BM.
source: Indeed, mice treated with IL7/aIL7 had significantly higher numbers of developing B cell subsets in the BM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), particularly of IL7-dependent proB and pre-B cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ALL numbers in BM were significantly reduced in mice treated with IL7/aIL7.
source: Conversely, ALL numbers in BM were significantly reduced, which reflected in significant reductions in peripheral blood and spleen (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The lymphotoxin-mediated attenuation of IL7 production reduces lymphopoiesis, which results in accelerated ALL growth.
source: Combined, these data demonstrate that the lymphotoxin-mediated attenuation of IL7 production reduces lymphopoiesis, which results in accelerated ALL growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the IL7/aIL7 treatment experiments.

claim: Artemis-deficient pre-B cells express significantly higher amounts of LTα and LTβ transcripts than Rag1-deficient pre-B cells.
source: Consistent with this possibility, when comparing the transcriptome of Artemis-deficient (Dclre1c−/−) and Rag1-deficient (Rag1−/−) pre-B cells, we noted that Artemis-deficient pre-B cells also expressed significantly higher amounts of LTα and LTβ transcripts (Bredemeyer et al., 2008; Bednarski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on analysis of published transcriptome data, supported by citations.

claim: Dclre1c−/− pre-B cells express higher amounts of LTα and LTβ protein on the cell surface than Rag1−/− pre-B cells.
source: In agreement with these observations, we detected higher amounts of LTα and LTβ protein on the cell surface of Dclre1c−/− pre-B cells than on Rag1−/− pre-B cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Transplantation of Dclre1c−/− BM cells into lethally irradiated Il7GFP/+ LTβR∆ mice or control littermate revealed LTβR-dependent Il7 downregulation.
source: Transplantation of Dclre1c−/− BM cells into lethally irradiated Il7GFP/+ LTβR∆ mice or control littermate revealed LTβR-dependent Il7 downregulation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), which resulted in a trend towards increased numbers of Artemis-deficient B cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Artemis deficiency did not impact myeloid-erythroid production.
source: In contrast, Artemis deficiency did not impact myeloid-erythroid production (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: ALLs upregulated LTα on the cell surface in an Etoposide dose-response manner.
source: To test if the DNA damage response controls LTα and LTβ expression, we treated ALL cells with Etoposide, a chemotherapeutic agent that prevents DSB repair. ALLs upregulated LTα on the cell surface in an Etoposide dose-response manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Treatment with IMD0354 (a small molecule inhibitor of IKKβ-mediated IκB phosphorylation) significantly reduced lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in Etoposide-treated ALLs.
source: Interestingly, treatment with IMD0354 (a small molecule inhibitor of IKKβ-mediated IκB phosphorylation) significantly reduced lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in Etoposide-treated ALLs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H.

claim: LTα and LTβ expression can be activated by DNA damage response pathway.
source: Combined, these studies demonstrate that LTα and LTβ expression can be activated by DNA damage response pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the Etoposide and IMD0354 treatment experiments.

claim: Gαi-protein coupled receptor signaling in B-lineage cells promotes lymphotoxin α1β2 expression.
source: Prior studies have shown that Gαi-protein coupled receptor signaling in B-lineage cells promotes lymphotoxin α1β2 expression (Ansel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Engagement of LTβR expressed on secondary lymphoid organ stromal cells increases the production of B cell chemokines, which further increases lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in B cells, thus establishing a feedforward loop.
source: Engagement of LTβR expressed on secondary lymphoid organ stromal cells increases the production of B cell chemokines, which further increases lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in B cells, thus establishing a feedforward loop (Ansel et al., 2000; Cyster et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ALLs upregulated LTα after exposure to CXCL12 in vitro.
source: To test if CXCR4 signaling in ALLs promotes lymphotoxin α1β2 expression, we treated ALLs in vitro with a range of CXCL12 concentrations and measured surface LTα. Indeed, ALLs upregulated LTα after exposure to CXCL12 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: LTα expression was further increased in ALLs treated with CXCL12 and Etoposide.
source: Furthermore, LTα expression was further increased in ALLs treated with CXCL12 and Etoposide (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: IL7R signaling can promote lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in lymphoid tissue inducer cells.
source: Although prior studies have also shown that IL7R signaling can promote lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in lymphoid tissue inducer cells (Yoshida et al., 2002), in ALL cells IL7R signaling was not sufficient for upregulating surface LTα even at high IL7 concentrations, even though it promoted IL7Ra internalization (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation, with new data showing it does not apply to ALL cells.

claim: In ALL cells IL7R signaling was not sufficient for upregulating surface LTα even at high IL7 concentrations.
source: Although prior studies have also shown that IL7R signaling can promote lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in lymphoid tissue inducer cells (Yoshida et al., 2002), in ALL cells IL7R signaling was not sufficient for upregulating surface LTα even at high IL7 concentrations, even though it promoted IL7Ra internalization (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Lymphotoxin α1β2 expression was significantly reduced in ALLs and in non-leukemic pre-B cells of AMD3100-treated mice.
source: To test if CXCR4 signaling is required for lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in ALLs in vivo, we transplanted 3×106 ALL cells into WT mice for 1 week and treated them with AMD3100, or saline, 12 hr prior to sacrifice. Indeed, lymphotoxin α1β2 expression was significantly reduced in ALLs and in non-leukemic pre-B cells of AMD3100-treated mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: AMD3100 increased CXCR4 surface expression in ALL and non-leukemic pre-B cells.
source: Conversely, AMD3100 increased CXCR4 surface expression in ALL and non-leukemic pre-B cells (Figure 5D), as expected (Broxmeyer et al., 2005; Beck et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: AMD3100 has a short half-life in vivo thus making it unsuitable for long-term treatment in vivo.
source: AMD3100 has a short half-life in vivo thus making it unsuitable for long-term treatment in vivo (Beck et al., 2014; Hendrix et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mice treated with CXCR4 antagonist maintained IL7 expression within the normal range of mice without ALL.
source: While control-treated mice showed ALL-induced Il7-GFP downregulation in MSCs, mice treated with CXCR4 antagonist maintained IL7 expression within the normal range of mice without ALL (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Developing B cells were significantly reduced in control-treated mice, but their numbers were normal in CXCR4 antagonist treated mice.
source: Similarly, developing B cells were significantly reduced in control-treated mice, but their numbers were normal in CXCR4 antagonist treated mice (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: ALL numbers were significantly decreased in the BM and periphery of mice treated with CXCR4 antagonist.
source: In contrast, ALL numbers were significantly decreased in the BM and periphery of mice treated with CXCR4 antagonist (Figure 5H), which correlated with extended mouse survival (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: CXCR4 antagonist treatment correlated with extended mouse survival after ALL transplantation.
source: In contrast, ALL numbers were significantly decreased in the BM and periphery of mice treated with CXCR4 antagonist (Figure 5H), which correlated with extended mouse survival (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: ALLs express significantly higher amounts of CXCR4 in vivo than non-leukemic B cell progenitors.
source: However, when comparing CXCR4 protein levels between ALLs and non-leukemic B cell progenitors developing in the same microenvironment, we noted that ALLs express significantly higher amounts of CXCR4 in vivo (Figure 5J) and migrate towards a CXCL12 gradient in vitro significantly more than non-leukemic developing B cell subsets (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: ALLs migrate towards a CXCL12 gradient in vitro significantly more than non-leukemic developing B cell subsets.
source: However, when comparing CXCR4 protein levels between ALLs and non-leukemic B cell progenitors developing in the same microenvironment, we noted that ALLs express significantly higher amounts of CXCR4 in vivo (Figure 5J) and migrate towards a CXCL12 gradient in vitro significantly more than non-leukemic developing B cell subsets (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: ALLs are retained more efficiently in the BM than non-leukemic B cell progenitors.
source: These observations suggest that ALLs are retained more efficiently in the BM than non-leukemic B cell progenitors.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher CXCR4 expression and migration data.

claim: AML induces the downregulation of multiple hematopoietic cytokines expressed by MSCs, including IL7.
source: As previously mentioned, AML also induces the downregulation of multiple hematopoietic cytokines expressed by MSCs, including IL7 (Baryawno et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: There is an inverse correlation between LTB transcript abundance and patient outcome in a cohort of AML patients from the Cancer Genome Atlas.
source: Furthermore, we also found an inverse correlation between LTB transcript abundance and patient outcome in a cohort of AML patients from the Cancer Genome Atlas (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A analyzing patient samples.

claim: MLL-AF9 expression increased the frequency of AML cells and of myeloid cell subsets expressing NGFR.
source: In a mixed BM chimera of DOX-induced MLL-AF9 transgenic and competitor WT cells expressing CD45.1, MLL-AF9 expression increased the frequency of AML cells and of myeloid cell subsets expressing NGFR, a reporter for MLL-AF9 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Both erythroid and lymphoid subsets were significantly reduced 2 and 4 weeks after MLL-AF9 induction.
source: In contrast, both erythroid and lymphoid subsets were significantly reduced 2 and 4 weeks after MLL-AF9 induction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: LTβ expression is higher on MLL-AF9-positive than on MLL-AF9-negative myeloid cells and neutrophils.
source: Next, we tested if the LTβR pathway is also engaged by AMLs. LTβ expression is higher on MLL-AF9-positive than on MLL-AF9-negative myeloid cells and neutrophils (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MLL-AF9-expressing cells induced IL7 downregulation in MSCs, which could be blocked with LTβR-Ig but not with Hel-Ig treatment.
source: MLL-AF9-expressing cells induced IL7 downregulation in MSCs, which could be blocked with LTβR-Ig but not with Hel-Ig treatment (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: LTβR-Ig treatment restored B lymphopoiesis partially in AML-bearing mice.
source: The effect of LTβR-Ig treatment also restored B lymphopoiesis partially (Figure 6C), but not erythropoiesis (Figure 6D), which correlated with reduced AML growth in vivo and extended mouse survival (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: LTβR-Ig treatment did not restore erythropoiesis in AML-bearing mice.
source: The effect of LTβR-Ig treatment also restored B lymphopoiesis partially (Figure 6C), but not erythropoiesis (Figure 6D), which correlated with reduced AML growth in vivo and extended mouse survival (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: LTβR-Ig treatment correlated with reduced AML growth in vivo and extended mouse survival.
source: The effect of LTβR-Ig treatment also restored B lymphopoiesis partially (Figure 6C), but not erythropoiesis (Figure 6D), which correlated with reduced AML growth in vivo and extended mouse survival (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: Acute lymphoid and myeloid leukemias turn off lymphopoiesis by expressing LTβR ligands and downregulating IL7 production.
source: Overall, these studies collectively demonstrate that acute lymphoid and myeloid leukemias turn off lymphopoiesis by expressing LTβR ligands and downregulating IL7 production.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the collective experimental data from ALL and AML studies.

claim: Leukemia cells physically interact with MSCs, which provides opportunities for LTβR engagement via membrane-bound lymphotoxin ligands.
source: The fact that AML and ALL cells physically interact with MSCs provides opportunities for LTβR engagement via membrane-bound lymphotoxin ligands.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and known biology.

claim: Artemis-deficient pre-B cells express elevated lymphotoxin α1β2.
source: Here, we demonstrated that the Artemis-deficient pre-B cells express elevated lymphotoxin α1β2 and that IL7 downregulation was dependent on LTβR signaling in MSCs.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: IL7 downregulation in Artemis-deficient pre-B cell model was dependent on LTβR signaling in MSCs.
source: Here, we demonstrated that the Artemis-deficient pre-B cells express elevated lymphotoxin α1β2 and that IL7 downregulation was dependent on LTβR signaling in MSCs.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The DSB sensing and repair pathway is one mechanism promoting lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in pre-leukemic cells through the activation of NFκB transcriptional activity.
source: These findings identify the DSB sensing and repair pathway as one mechanism promoting lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in pre-leukemic cells through the activation of NFκB transcriptional activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the Etoposide and IMD0354 treatment experiments.

claim: Upregulation of lymphotoxin α1β2 in pre-B cells carrying unrepaired DSBs promotes IL7 downregulation, which may contribute to the efficient elimination of pre-leukemic B cell progenitors in vivo.
source: Because upregulation of lymphotoxin α1β2 in pre-B cells carrying unrepaired DSBs promotes IL7 downregulation, we speculate that this mechanism may contribute to the efficient elimination of pre-leukemic B cell progenitors in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: CXCR4 signaling induces lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in ALL cells in vitro and in vivo.
source: Our studies revealed that CXCR4 signaling also induces lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in ALL cells in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 5A-D.

claim: CXCR4 expression levels in AML and ALL cells inversely correlate with patient outcome.
source: CXCL12 is the most abundant chemokine expressed by MSCs and ECs in BM, and CXCR4 expression levels in AML and ALL cells inversely correlate with patient outcome (Cancilla et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: CXCR4 signaling enables leukemic cell interactions and delivery of lymphotoxin α1β2 to MSCs and promotes further lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in leukemic cells in a feed-forward loop that shuts down IL7 expression and blocks lymphopoiesis.
source: We suggest that CXCR4 signaling not only enables leukemic cell interactions and delivery of lymphotoxin α1β2 to MSCs but also promote further lymphotoxin α1β2 expression in leukemic cells in a feed-forward loop that shuts down IL7 expression and blocks lymphopoiesis.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: The inverse correlation between lymphotoxin α1β2 expression and ALL and AML patient outcome is in agreement with data showing that CXCR4 and LTβR act in the same axis.
source: The fact that our studies also revealed an inverse correlation between lymphotoxin α1β2 expression and ALL and AML patient outcome, as has been described with CXCR4 (Cancilla et al., 2020), is in agreement with the data presented in this study showing that CXCR4 and LTβR act in the same axis.
evidence: This is an inference connecting patient outcome data with mechanistic findings.

claim: CXCL12 is downregulated in MSCs when AML develops.
source: Prior studies using mouse models of AML have shown that CXCL12 is downregulated in MSCs when AML develops (Baryawno et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: ALL cells induce a small but significant downregulation of CXCL12 expression in MSCs that is partly dependent on LTβR signaling.
source: Here, we showed that ALL cells induce a small but significant downregulation of CXCL12 expression in MSCs that is partly dependent on LTβR signaling.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: High CXCR4 levels confer competitive advantage over non-leukemic hematopoietic progenitors in BM retention and access to supportive microenvironments for cell growth.
source: We speculate that high CXCR4 levels confer competitive advantage over non-leukemic hematopoietic progenitors in BM retention and access to supportive microenvironments for cell growth.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: CAR-T cells engineered to express IL7 showed improved long-term persistence.
source: A recent study, however, showed that CAR-T engineered to express IL7 improved their long-term persistence (Adachi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: LTβR blocking in combination with CAR-T cell therapy particularly for B cell leukemias may improve CAR-T cell persistence by increasing IL7 production in BM while not affecting CXCL12 expression.
source: It is possible that LTβR blocking in combination with CAR-T cell therapy particularly for B cell leukemias may also improve CAR-T cell persistence by increasing IL7 production in BM while not affecting CXCL12 expression.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic implication of the findings.

claim: Of all hematopoietic cytokines downregulated by leukemic cells, only IL7 (and partly CXCL12) are regulated by LTβR signaling.
source: Of all hematopoietic cytokines downregulated by leukemic cells, only IL7 (and partly CXCL12) are regulated by LTβR signaling.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SCF is a critical cytokine for the survival and expansion of myelo-erythroid lineage progenitors.
source: Of note, SCF is a critical cytokine for the survival and expansion of myelo-erythroid lineage progenitors (Miao et al., 2020; Broudy et al., 1995; Broudy, 1997; Munugalavadla and Kapur, 2005), and its consumption in vivo is under competition between hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (Miao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SCF consumption in vivo is under competition between hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells.
source: Of note, SCF is a critical cytokine for the survival and expansion of myelo-erythroid lineage progenitors (Miao et al., 2020; Broudy et al., 1995; Broudy, 1997; Munugalavadla and Kapur, 2005), and its consumption in vivo is under competition between hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (Miao et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SCF production is insensitive to LTβR signaling, which may contribute to explain why myelopoiesis and erythropoiesis are not restored when LTβR signaling is blocked.
source: The fact that SCF production is insensitive to LTβR signaling may contribute to explain why myelopoiesis and erythropoiesis are not restored when LTβR signaling is blocked.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and known biology of SCF.

claim: Additional receptor(s)/ligand(s) interaction(s) may be responsible for controlling the production of other hematopoietic cytokines besides IL7.
source: These findings also raise the possibility that additional receptor(s)/ligand(s) interaction(s) are responsible for controlling the production of other hematopoietic cytokines.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.
